memory_update.text: Energy theme should be treated as an electrification, reliability, and grid/nuclear bottleneck map, not as only oil/gas or uranium commodity exposure.
Transmission-line hardware is a high-priority underfollowed discovery node because utility-qualified fittings and conductor accessories may have specification lock-in and limited analyst attention.
Transformers, dry-type transformers, magnetics, and power-quality equipment are central nodes for AI data centers, industrial electrification, renewables, microgrids, and aging-grid replacement.

HVDC, FACTS, reactors, harmonic filters, STATCOM, and high-voltage power-quality components are promising global underfollowed supplier lanes due to long qualification cycles and limited qualified suppliers.
Nuclear fuel-cycle middle steps, especially conversion, enrichment, HALEU, and fabrication, deserve separate analysis from uranium mining and SMR developer narratives.
Layer 1B should verify candidate companies using primary filings, segment revenue, backlog, customer evidence, certifications, qualification claims, and market-cap/coverage data.

layer1a.summary: Energy should be decomposed first as an electrification and reliability bottleneck theme rather than a single commodity trade. The broad demand stack is AI/data-center load growth, industrial reshoring, electrification, renewable interconnection, aging grid replacement, nuclear restart/SMR optionality, and energy-security policy. The highest-quality Layer 1A decomposition points toward scarce physical grid equipment, transmission construction hardware, nuclear fuel-cycle capacity, high-voltage power-quality systems, transformer and power-distribution equipment, and niche EPC/testing/certification suppliers. Obvious reference leaders such as hyperscalers, large utilities, nuclear owners, turbine OEMs, and mega-cap electrical equipment companies are useful for demand validation, but the discovery lane should deliberately search one or two layers upstream for small/mid-cap suppliers with qualification moats, utility specification lock-in, low analyst coverage, and hidden customer dependencies.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The bottleneck is not only miles of transmission built, but the availability of utility-qualified, specification-embedded hardware with decades of field reliability. Supplier switching can require engineering review and requalification, creating sticky share for incumbent niche suppliers.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer $300M-$3B niche industrials with direct grid-hardware revenue, high domestic manufacturing content, and visible backlog/order growth. Treat micro-caps as speculative unless filings show durable utility customers and positive cash generation.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Transmission-line hardware, conductor fittings, clamps, spacers, dead-ends, vibration dampers, and line accessories
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Search for companies with product catalogs embedded in utility specifications, high insider ownership, limited Wall Street coverage, long operating histories, and exposure to both utility transmission and communications/fiber infrastructure.
search_queries: "Preformed Line Products" transmission hardware analyst coverage
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: This node is usually ignored because investors focus on utilities, EPC contractors, and large electrical OEMs, while the bill-of-materials hardware suppliers may have cleaner exposure to grid volume and lower narrative saturation.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: New generation, data-center load, renewable interconnection, and grid hardening all require physical transmission and distribution hardware. These parts are small relative to total project cost but mandatory for line reliability and utility acceptance.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: Transformer and magnetics capacity may remain constrained because demand is broad-based while manufacturing requires specialized design, electrical steel/magnetics expertise, safety certification, and customer qualification.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Target $500M-$10B public companies where transformer/power-quality revenue is material. Avoid names where the exposure is buried inside a diversified conglomerate unless segment disclosure is strong.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Transformers, dry-type transformers, magnetics, power conditioning, and medium-voltage distribution equipment
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Look for small/mid-cap transformer manufacturers with North American capacity, exposure to digital infrastructure and industrial electrification, pricing power, backlog expansion, and acquisitions that broaden them from component makers into electrification platforms.
search_queries: "power quality products" transformer manufacturer public company
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: The market often labels these companies as boring industrials rather than AI/electrification enablers, creating a second-order beneficiary lane.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Data centers, semiconductor fabs, industrial electrification, renewables, EV charging, and microgrids all need equipment to step voltage up/down, condition power, and distribute electricity safely inside facilities and across local grids.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: HVDC/FACTS and high-voltage power-quality components are scarce because there are few qualified suppliers, reliability standards are strict, project qualification cycles are long, and customers are sticky once products are approved.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer $300M-$5B companies with documented HVDC/FACTS products, export customers, utility approvals, and growing high-voltage order books. Watch liquidity and governance quality in emerging-market listings.
supply_chain_nodes.node: HVDC, FACTS, high-voltage reactors, harmonic filters, STATCOM systems, instrument transformers, and grid power-quality equipment
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Search globally, not only in the U.S. Many underfollowed suppliers may be listed in India, Canada, Europe, Japan, Korea, or Taiwan and may sell to larger OEMs such as GE, Siemens, Hitachi Energy, Hyosung, or national grid operators.
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: These companies may be hidden as component suppliers to larger grid OEMs, so the customer relationship rather than the brand name may reveal the bottleneck.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Long-distance renewable transmission, grid stability, industrial loads, and high-density data centers increase the need for equipment that manages reactive power, harmonics, voltage stability, and bulk power transfer.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The investable bottleneck may be less about raw uranium mining and more about conversion, enrichment, and HALEU capacity, because those steps require specialized facilities, licensing, long lead times, and policy support.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer companies where fuel-cycle revenue or contracted capacity is visible. Include $300M-$10B names first; treat pre-revenue nuclear technology firms as speculative_shadow unless they have funded contracts, licenses, or strategic customers.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Nuclear fuel-cycle bottlenecks: uranium conversion, enrichment, HALEU, fabrication, and related licensing
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Use uranium miners and large nuclear operators as context, but search specifically for companies tied to enrichment technology, domestic fuel-cycle rebuilding, HALEU contracts, conversion capacity, fabrication, deconversion, and government funding awards.
search_queries: "domestic nuclear fuel" enrichment contract public company
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: Public debate often centers on uranium spot prices or SMR press releases, while the harder-to-scale fuel-cycle middle steps may determine which projects are executable.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Nuclear restarts, life extensions, new large reactors, and SMR ambitions require a functioning fuel cycle. Reactor announcements cannot translate into electricity without mined uranium, conversion, enrichment, fabrication, and licensed logistics.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The bottleneck may sit in qualified suppliers and service providers that can meet nuclear QA standards rather than in reactor developers themselves. Qualification barriers and small supplier populations may create pricing power.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer profitable $500M-$10B industrials with nuclear-qualified revenue. Large-cap references are useful, but the discovery target is a smaller supplier with a material nuclear segment and repeat service demand.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Nuclear-qualified components, reactor parts, pumps, valves, forgings, inspection, testing, and specialty field services
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Search for companies with ASME nuclear certifications, N-stamp capabilities, NRC-related services, long-term utility customers, defense nuclear crossover exposure, and outage/refueling service revenue.
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: Nuclear component suppliers can be obscured inside industrial labels, defense supply chains, or maintenance-service categories, while attention goes to utilities and SMR developers.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Nuclear assets require certified components and services with stringent safety, documentation, quality-assurance, and regulatory requirements. Life extensions and uprates can drive demand before new reactors arrive.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: Large EPC leaders may capture investor attention, but smaller specialty service providers with scarce crews, testing expertise, or regional utility relationships may benefit from grid capex without carrying the same mega-project execution risk.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer $300M-$5B service firms with recurring utility revenue, backlog visibility, and conservative balance sheets. Be cautious of cyclicality, labor inflation, accident risk, and low-margin contract structures.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Grid EPC subcontractors, utility field services, testing, commissioning, maintenance, vegetation management, and specialized labor
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Search for publicly listed contractors and service firms with utility T&D exposure, storm hardening, substation commissioning, testing labs, grid maintenance, vegetation management, and recurring service contracts.
search_queries: "transmission distribution services" small cap public company
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: This is a second-order capacity bottleneck: not the equipment itself, but the people and certification processes required to install, energize, inspect, and maintain it.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: Even when equipment is available, projects can be delayed by permitting, engineering, skilled labor, testing, commissioning, interconnection studies, and field execution capacity.

demand_drivers: AI and cloud data centers increasing electricity demand and requiring reliable, dispatchable power
Grid interconnection backlogs and transmission buildout needed for renewables, data centers, industrial load, and electrification
Aging North American grid infrastructure requiring replacement of transformers, substations, conductors, hardware, protection systems, and power-quality equipment
Nuclear life extensions, restarts, new reactor interest, and SMR announcements increasing attention on uranium conversion, enrichment, HALEU, fabrication, and nuclear-qualified components
Industrial reshoring, semiconductor fabs, EV charging, microgrids, oil/gas electrification, and process automation increasing demand for medium/high-voltage electrical infrastructure
Energy-security policy and domestic supply-chain reshoring driving interest in U.S./North American grid and nuclear fuel-cycle suppliers

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Use a two-lane Serenity funnel. Lane 1 uses reference leaders to validate demand: hyperscalers, nuclear generators, large utilities, turbine OEMs, EPC firms, and large electrical-equipment companies. Lane 2 searches for underfollowed suppliers whose products are mandatory but less visible: transmission fittings, conductor hardware, dry-type transformers, power-quality equipment, HVDC/FACTS components, nuclear fuel-cycle services, nuclear-qualified components, grid testing/inspection, substation automation, and niche distributors. Prefer public companies in the roughly $300M-$10B market-cap range when exposure is direct and evidence can be tied to filings, customer disclosures, qualification claims, backlog, or segment growth.
supply_side_constraints: Long qualification and reliability testing cycles for grid hardware, transformers, HVDC/FACTS equipment, nuclear components, and fuel-cycle assets
Limited qualified supplier bases in utility-grade transmission hardware, transformers, high-voltage reactors, harmonic filters, switchgear, and nuclear fuel-cycle services
Permitting, regulatory licensing, and safety requirements for transmission lines, nuclear facilities, enrichment, conversion, and reactor components
Physical manufacturing capacity constraints in transformers, electrical steel/magnetics, high-voltage components, and grid construction services
Utility specification lock-in and high switching costs for mission-critical hardware used in decades-long grid assets
Project execution bottlenecks in EPC, specialized labor, testing, inspection, certification, and field services
